title: Hardware asset lifecycle
prompt: A company buys new laptops that will store confidential data and will eventually be retired. Order the asset management activities from first to last across the laptops' lifecycle.

items.text: Purchase through the approved procurement process
items.why: Acquisition comes first; approved vendors and processes reduce supply chain and shadow IT risk.

items.text: Assign an owner and a data classification
items.why: Once received, each asset gets an accountable owner and a classification that drives its protection.

items.text: Audit the inventory periodically while in use
items.why: Once the laptop is assigned and in use, monitoring and asset tracking (periodic inventory audits, enumeration) keep it visible until it is retired.

items.text: Archive data required by the retention policy
items.why: At decommissioning, data that must be retained is preserved before the media is touched; wiping it first could breach legal or policy obligations.

items.text: Sanitize or destroy the storage media
items.why: Data is removed (wiping, crypto-erase) or the media is physically destroyed so it cannot be recovered.
Certification is the final proof that disposal was carried out, and it is kept for audit purposes.

explanation: SY0-701 4.2 follows the asset from acquisition/procurement, through assignment/accounting (ownership, classification) and monitoring/asset tracking, to disposal/decommissioning. During disposal, data covered by retention requirements is archived before sanitization or destruction (wiping first would destroy it), and certification documents the result. The objectives list these as bullets, not a sequence, so order them by what each step depends on.

title: Vulnerability management lifecycle
prompt: A security team is running its monthly vulnerability management cycle for the server fleet. Order the activities from first to last.

items.why: Identification comes first: you cannot fix what you have not found.

items.text: Confirm findings to rule out false positives
items.why: Analysis begins by confirming each finding, so no effort is wasted on issues that do not exist.

items.text: Prioritize by CVSS, exposure and asset value
items.why: Confirmed findings are ranked using severity and environmental factors, so the riskiest are fixed first.

items.text: Patch or apply a compensating control
items.why: Response and remediation address the prioritized vulnerabilities, using patching, segmentation, an exception or insurance.
Validation proves that the fix worked; a remediation is not finished until it has been verified.
Reporting closes the cycle by documenting status, trends and accepted exceptions for management.

explanation: SY0-701 4.3 structures vulnerability management as identification, analysis (confirmation, then prioritization with CVSS, exposure factor, environmental variables and risk tolerance), response and remediation, validation of remediation (rescanning, audit, verification) and reporting. A remediation is only complete after a rescan confirms it.

title: Secure protocols and default ports
prompt: A firewall administrator is writing the allow list for a hardened server zone that may only use encrypted protocols. Match each secure protocol to its default port. Some ports will not be used.

pairs.why: SSH listens on TCP 22; SFTP and SCP run inside SSH, so they share the port.
HTTP over TLS uses TCP 443, replacing cleartext HTTP on TCP 80.
LDAP over TLS uses TCP 636; cleartext LDAP uses TCP 389.
IMAP over TLS uses TCP 993; cleartext IMAP uses TCP 143.
POP3 over TLS uses TCP 995; cleartext POP3 uses TCP 110.

explanation: Port selection is part of enforcing secure protocols: the allow list should permit the TLS/SSH ports and block the cleartext equivalents (LDAP 389, IMAP 143, POP3 110). Two unused ports are cleartext LDAP and IMAP; TCP 990 is implicit FTPS, which is encrypted but is not one of the listed protocols. Knowing each secure port next to its insecure counterpart is the fastest way to spot a misconfigured rule on the exam.

title: Access control models in practice
prompt: An identity architect is documenting how access decisions are made across several systems. Match each scenario to the access control model it describes. One option will not be used.

pairs.why: MAC compares administrator-assigned labels and clearances; users cannot change them.

pairs.left: A file's creator chooses who may read it
pairs.why: DAC lets the owner of the object grant or revoke access at their discretion.

pairs.left: All nurses get the same chart permissions
pairs.why: RBAC assigns permissions to a job role, and users inherit them by being placed in that role.
ABAC evaluates multiple attributes of the user, device and context in a policy.

pairs.left: Router ACL applies equally to every user
pairs.why: Rule-based access control applies administrator-defined rules to all subjects regardless of identity.

explanation: Look for the deciding factor: labels and clearances mean MAC, owner choice means DAC, job function means RBAC, a combination of user/device/context attributes means ABAC, and a uniform rule set such as an ACL means rule-based access control. Time-of-day restrictions are unused because no scenario limits access by time.

title: MFA factor categories
prompt: An IAM engineer is designing MFA policies and must make sure each login combines different factor categories. Classify each authenticator by its factor.

items.why: A memorized secret: something you know.
Recalled information: something you know.

items.text: TOTP code from an authenticator app
items.why: The code proves possession of the device holding the seed: something you have.

items.text: Smart card inserted into a reader
items.why: A physical token in the user's possession: something you have.
A hardware authenticator the user carries: something you have.
A physical characteristic of the user: biometric, something you are.

items.text: GPS shows the device inside headquarters
items.why: The user's physical location is the factor: somewhere you are.

explanation: MFA requires factors from different categories; a password plus a PIN is still single-factor because both are something you know. Codes from authenticator apps, SMS or hardware tokens count as something you have because they prove possession of a device, even though the user types them. Location (GPS, IP geolocation) is somewhere you are.

title: Order of volatility on a live server
prompt: A responder arrives at a compromised web server that is still powered on and connected. Policy requires preserving as much evidence as possible. Order the evidence sources from the one that must be collected first to the one that can be collected last.

items.why: Contents change within nanoseconds as instructions execute, so they are the most volatile source.
Survives only while the system stays powered; lost at shutdown and constantly overwritten.
Short-lived by design (often RAM-backed, or cleared at reboot or by routine cleanup), so they rank above regular disk data.
Persists across reboots; changes slowly unless actively overwritten.
Stored off the host (e.g. SIEM/syslog), so the attacker on this server is less likely to alter it, but retention windows still apply.
Offline or long-term storage that changes least; it can safely be collected last.

explanation: The order of volatility (as described in RFC 3227 and used by CompTIA) says to collect the evidence that disappears fastest first. Pulling the plug before capturing memory destroys running processes, injected code, keys and open connections. Remote logs and archives are least volatile, so they are collected after the volatile data on the host.

title: Incident response process
prompt: A company is writing its incident response plan and wants the phases to match CompTIA's incident response process. Order the phases from first to last.

items.why: Plans, playbooks, tooling and training are put in place before any incident occurs.
An alert, report or anomaly reveals that a possible incident is occurring.
Responders confirm it is a real incident and work out its scope, impact and severity.
Limits the spread and damage (isolate hosts, block IOCs) before the threat is removed.
Removes the cause: malware, persistence, compromised accounts and the exploited vulnerability.
Restores systems to normal, validated operation and monitors for recurrence.
A post-incident review improves the plan, controls and preparation for the next incident.

explanation: SY0-701 lists the process as Preparation, Detection, Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery and Lessons learned. Exam technique: when a question asks what to do FIRST after an incident is confirmed, the answer is usually containment, which comes before eradication and recovery.
industryVsComptia: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 groups these into four phases (Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-incident activity). The SY0-701 objectives list each step separately, so use the seven-step order on the exam.

title: Investigation questions and data sources
prompt: An analyst is investigating a suspected intrusion and has several specific questions. Match each question to the data source that BEST answers it. One source will not be used.

pairs.left: Was traffic to TCP 445 allowed or denied?
pairs.why: Firewall logs record the allow/deny decision for each connection, with source, destination and port.

pairs.left: What exact payload crossed the wire?
pairs.why: Only a packet capture contains the full contents of the traffic, not just a summary of it.

pairs.left: Which mail servers relayed this email?
pairs.why: Email headers are metadata; the Received lines show each relay hop and timestamp.

pairs.left: Did a known exploit signature fire?
pairs.why: IDS/IPS logs record signature matches for known attack patterns.

pairs.left: Which unpatched CVEs exist on the servers?
pairs.why: A vulnerability scan enumerates missing patches and known CVEs on each host.

pairs.left: Who logged on to the workstation at 2 a.m.?
pairs.why: The operating system's security log records interactive logon events with account and time.

explanation: Match the question to the source that records that evidence natively: decisions in firewall logs, content in packet captures, routing details in email metadata, signature hits in IDS/IPS logs, weaknesses in scan results and logons in OS security logs. A dashboard aggregates other sources for visibility but is not the BEST source for any single detailed question.
